title: Elijah
lead: Elijah the Tishbite, the prophet of the LORD in the days of Ahab and Jezebel (about 870–850 BC), shut the sky, raised a widow's son, faced the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel and met God at Horeb. He was taken up to heaven without dying, and Malachi promised he would return before the day of the LORD, so Jews await him at every Passover and Christians saw his coming in John the Baptist.

sections.b:
Elijah appears without warning to announce a drought (1 Kings 17:1). He is fed by ravens and by a widow of Zarephath, whose son he raises (1 Kings 17). On Carmel he calls down fire and Israel cries, "The LORD, he is the God!" (1 Kings 18:39). Threatened by Jezebel, he flees to Horeb, where the LORD meets him not in wind, quake or fire but in "a sound of thin silence" (1 Kings 19:12), and he calls Elisha. He condemns Ahab over Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21) and Ahaziah over Baal-zebub (2 Kings 1), and is taken up in a whirlwind with chariots of fire (2 Kings 2:11). Chronicles adds a letter he wrote to King Jehoram (2 Chronicles 21:12–15).

Malachi closes the prophets with the promise, "Look, I am sending you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the LORD's day, the great and fearful day" (Malachi 4:5), to turn the hearts of parents and children. Ben Sira praises him as a prophet "like fire" (Sirach 48:1–11).

sections.b: The gospels ask whether John the Baptist is Elijah. Luke says John will "walk ahead of the Lord with Elijah's spirit and power" (Luke 1:17); Jesus says that if they will accept it, John "is Elijah who is to come" (Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:10–13); John himself denies being Elijah (John 1:21), probably meaning he is not Elijah returned in person. Some thought Jesus was Elijah (Mark 6:15; Mark 8:28). Moses and Elijah appear with Jesus at the Transfiguration (Mark 9:2–8), and bystanders at the cross think Jesus is calling Elijah (Mark 15:35–36). Jesus recalls the widow of Zarephath (Luke 4:25–26), Paul the seven thousand (Romans 11:2–4), and James Elijah's prayer (James 5:17–18). Revelation's two witnesses have Elijah's power to shut the sky (Revelation 11:6).

sections.h: Elijah in Jewish and Islamic tradition
sections.b: Because the Bible does not record his death, Jewish tradition made Elijah a living helper of Israel: he visits the poor, teaches the sages, and will settle every unsolved question of law when he comes. At the Passover meal a cup is poured for him and the door opened, and at every circumcision a chair is set for him (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 29). The Mishnah says he will come to make peace (Mishnah Eduyot 8:7). Some traditions identify him with Phinehas, the zealous priest (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 47). The Qur'an names Ilyas among the messengers, who called his people away from Ba'l (Qur'an 37:123–132).

Many early Christian writers expected Elijah to return in person before Christ's second coming, often with Enoch, as the two witnesses of Revelation 11, since neither had died (Hippolytus, On Christ and Antichrist 43; Tertullian, On the Soul 50). Eastern Orthodox churches keep the feast of the Prophet Elias on July 20, and many hilltop chapels in Greece bear his name. The Carmelite order, which began with hermits on Mount Carmel around 1200, honors Elijah as its spiritual father (see Mount Carmel).
